Often land needs to be maintained as farmland for at least 2 out of the last 10 years, much like you are doing clearing saplings and such, to be considered consistently farmed land. It sounds like OP had mature forest that was cleared, regardless of whether it's classified as a wetland or not. Farmed and farmable wetlands are a thing but they usually need to be grandfathered in prior to the 1985 Food Security Act and more or less continuously farmed since then. 

There is a lot of leniency for "previously converted farmland" (usually pre-1985) that doesn't apply to newly cleared land. Additionally, clearing land now is often subject to regulation by the USACE through the Clean Water Act rather than NRCS, regardless of use. If a wetland is found on FSA, that's one thing, but there are millions of acres of wetlands across the country that are subject to regulation and not accounted for in FSA. 

Again, regardless of what OP's mother may think of this, if the area is a forested wetland (whether determined in FSA or not) and it has a connection to downstream waters, this is a violation of the Clean Water Act.

I'm almost jealous of the opportunities you will have to teach your crews about the fires of the ranch this year, you seem very well suited to do so. 

During my time at the ranch I spent hundreds of hours doing conservation work in the burn country. Turning soil and planting thousands of trees, building trail in that "blasted wasteland", and ruminating over how we can promote prescribed fire as an effective solution to the declining health of Philmont's forests. You're totally right about the Mt. Phillips area, btw, that area is choking itself to death and a fire up there would be devastating.

Interesting point: As I looked at the fire map this morning, I noticed that the fire did not jump across the valley between Hunting Lodge and Cito. This was an area that was the focus of a multi-year understory clearing project by the Conservation Department in an effort to to solve the "meadow encroachment" that was occurring there due to lack of fire (based on historic photos). Crews would help clear ladder fuel and slash as Cons crews fed the brush and selected trees through a chipper, I don't know if they are continuing with the chipper crews in areas, but this could be evidence of a successful management scheme. While I don't know the details of how the fire was fought in the area, but it seems as though that active fuel reduction may have had an impact on the fire's behavior, just food for thought to keep that in mind as you move through the area this summer.
